title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E526 derives the transverse (Euler–Bernoulli) vibration modes of elastic rods and laminae for free, simply supported ('simpliciter fixa') and clamped ('firmiter infixa') ends. The frequency comes out proportional to c/a^2 times a material constant (Euler's b), where a is the length and c a thickness parameter. Corollary 2 on the previous page states that for similar cross-sections the pitch is proportional to c/a^2.

This page (end of Scholion §46): For a rectangular cross-section ABCD there are two principal bending directions. If the rod bends about the axis AB (lines AC and BD are bent), Euler's c equals the side AC. If it bends about AC, c equals AB. In each case the other side does not enter at all. So the tones go as AC/a^2 or AB/a^2.

In modern terms: ω_n = (β_n L)^2 sqrt(EI/(ρA))/L^2. For a rectangle, sqrt(I/A) = h/sqrt(12), where h is the dimension in the plane of bending. The width cancels, so frequency ∝ h/L^2. This is correct.

For a circular section of diameter AB, Euler asserts c = (3/4)·AB, independent of the bending axis (isotropy). He then remarks that only free, pinned and clamped ends have been treated. A rod may also be pinned at one or more interior points without destroying the coupling of the parts. Treating all such cases would be an infinite task, so one representative case is added.

Problem §47: a rod is simply supported at both ends E and F and also pinned by a stylus at an arbitrary interior point L. Find all its vibration modes. The next page sets up the solution:
- Write EL = λa.
- Use separate solutions y = α e^{uω} + β e^{-uω} + γ sin uω + δ cos uω on each span, with a common time factor.
- At L impose y = 0 and continuity of dy/ds and d²y/ds² (slope and bending moment).
This is the modern treatment of a two-span continuous beam on three supports, leading to a transcendental frequency equation in ω depending on λ.
errors: Circular section: with c defined so that frequency ∝ c/a^2 and c equal to the thickness of a rectangle, equivalence requires c^2/12 = d^2/16 (equal radii of gyration about the centroidal axis). This gives c^2 = (3/4)d^2, i.e. c = (√3/2)·AB ≈ 0.866·AB, not c = (3/4)·AB as printed. Euler (or his amanuensis or the printer) appears to have confused c with c^2. It would be worth checking against how c enters the earlier formulas of E526 and any Opera omnia note; if c there is the rectangular thickness, the printed 3/4 is an error.

ideas.what: Frequency of a rectangular bar depends only on the dimension in the plane of bending, not on the width; two principal bending planes give two families of tones
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli beam frequency ∝ radius of gyration / L^2; principal flexural axes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Daniel Bernoulli (1730s–1740s); experimental confirmation by Chladni (1787)
ideas.where_published: E526 itself; frequency scaling for laminae already in Euler's 1744 Additamentum De curvis elasticis (E65)

ideas.what: Reduction of a circular cross-section to an equivalent thickness parameter c (via the moment of inertia of the section)
ideas.modern_name: Equivalent rectangular thickness via the area moment of inertia / radius of gyration
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; the general section-stiffness concept is later systematized by Navier and Saint-Venant

ideas.what: Vibrations of a rod pinned at the ends and at an arbitrary interior point, with continuity of slope and moment and zero displacement at the support
ideas.modern_name: Free vibration of a two-span continuous beam (intermediate simple support)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Usually discussed in 19th-century texts (Rayleigh's Theory of Sound, Clebsch); Euler's priority is recorded by Truesdell
ideas.where_published: E526 §47ff (Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1779/1782); discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (O.O. II.11.2)

missed.claim: The numerical factor for the circular cross-section (c = 3/4 of the diameter) appears inconsistent with the correct value √3/2 ≈ 0.866. This possible small slip seems not to be widely noted in secondary literature.
missed.quote: tum pro formulis noſtris erit c = 3/4 A B
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of historical-editorial interest: it bears on how Euler computed sectional stiffness in 1779, by the centroidal axis versus older edge-axis conventions.

deep.surprise_reason: Standard material from a well-studied paper, covered by Truesdell. The only notable point is a likely factor error (3/4 versus √3/2) for the circular section. The intermediate-support problem is known to be in E526.
transcription_corrections: 'venitur' as printed in the image is likely a misprint for 'venit'; the transcription faithfully reproduces the image.
'A C.,' has a spurious period in the transcription; the image reads 'A C,'.
